title: The Physician at the King's Elbow: Cnidus, Cunaxa, and the Books of Marvels
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cnidus, born on the long peninsula
stops.date_confidence: birthplace attested, birth year not. Strabo, Geography 14.2.15, is explicit that Ctesias came from Cnidus. No ancient source gives a year. Livius.org offers a modern estimate of 444-434 BC, reckoned backward from an assumed capture around 414; T. S. Brown's often-cited 441 is a separate modern calculation, made to leave room for a medical training, and is not an ancient datum. The 440 here is an ordering device standing inside the modern range, not a claim. Month and day default. Coordinates are the excavated site of Knidos in Yazikoy, Mugla province, matching the pin used for the site elsewhere.
stops.campa: A son is born to a Cnidian house on the long finger of rock that runs west into the sea between two gulfs. The city is Dorian, Greek in speech and law, and it sits inside the reach of the Great King, whose satraps hold the coast at its back. No ancient writer gives the year of the birth. The figures in circulation are all modern, reckoned backward from a capture that cannot be dated either. What antiquity records of the origin is one line in Strabo, written four centuries afterward: the man was from Cnidus.
suggested_refs: The excavated site of Knidos on the Datca peninsula, dug by Charles Thomas Newton in 1857-58
sources: Strabo, Geography 14.2.15, Loeb translation at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Cnidus, the father named twice
stops.date_confidence: the father's name is attested but not stable. The Suda calls him Ctesiarchus; a second strand of the tradition, including Lucian's preface to the True History, calls him Ctesiochus. No source reconciles the two and this file does not either. The date is an ordering device with no evidential content; nothing whatever is recorded about the household or the childhood.
stops.campa: Later lexicography gives him a father and then cannot hold the name still. The Suda calls the man Ctesiarchus. Another strand of the tradition calls him Ctesiochus, and Lucian, five centuries on, uses that second form when he lists the Cnidian among the great liars. Which spelling the household itself used, no ancient source troubles to settle. Nothing else of that household comes down: no mother, no brother, no teacher's name, no property, no office, no notice of a childhood.
suggested_refs: The Suda, Adler kappa 2521, the entry on Ctesias

stops.name: Cnidus, the school that was not Cos
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That Cnidus had a famous body of physicians called Asclepiads is attested (livius.org, 'Ctesias of Cnidus'), and that Ctesias practised medicine is attested by Strabo, Xenophon and Diodorus alike. That he trained in a Cnidian school as a rival of the Coan school is the standard modern reconstruction; no ancient text describes his training, names a teacher, or places him at an Asclepieion. An earlier draft of this file carried a separate Asclepieion pin about seven hundred metres from the city; there is nothing behind that coordinate and it has been collapsed into the city pin. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Cnidus keeps physicians of its own, the Asclepiads, who trace the craft to the god. They disagree with the Coans about how a body is to be read and handled, and the boy is trained here, in the rival house. No ancient text describes that training: no teacher named, no case book, no Asclepieion. Later readers assign him to Cnidus because they find him arguing against Coan doctrine rather than repeating it. Across the narrow water lies Cos, and on Cos the school of Hippocrates.
suggested_refs: The Cnidian medical writings, known only through their opponents and through Galen

stops.name: Cnidus, hellebore safer than in his father's day
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and weakly sourced. The two medical remarks, the criticism of the Hippocratic method of reducing a dislocated hip and the observation about hellebore, are reported as Galenic testimonia in the modern literature on Ctesias (Schmitt, Encyclopaedia Iranica; Nichols 2011). The Iranica article returned 403 on the research pass and livius.org mentions neither Galen nor hip dislocation, so neither remark could be traced to a fetchable text of Galen. Carried as a reconstruction with the gap declared. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Galen, keeping what he can of the Cnidian physicians, preserves a remark of Ctesias about hellebore: a drug that killed in his father's time, and that the doctors of his own generation give without the same fear, because they have learned how to prepare it. The same testimony has him faulting the Hippocratic method for putting back a dislocated hip. Those two remarks are the whole of his surviving medical work. Neither can be traced now to a text of Galen a reader can open; both arrive through modern editors reporting what Galen reported.
suggested_refs: Galen's citations of Ctesias among the Cnidian physicians
sources: Ruediger Schmitt, Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Ctesias' (403 on this pass, relayed through secondary summaries)

stops.name: Sardis, the disputed capture
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout, and the weakest pin on this itinerary. Diodorus 2.32.4 attests only that Ctesias was made prisoner and retained for his medical knowledge; he names no battle, no captor and no place. The tie to Cnidus changing allegiance in the Peloponnesian War, to the revolt of Pissuthnes, and to capture by Tissaphernes is T. S. Brown's hypothesis of 1978, defended in part by Jan Stronk; Dominique Lenfant's BMCR review of 2012.04.27 confirms the attribution of the hypothesis to Brown but not the hypothesis itself. Sardis is the satrapal seat of Lydia and is chosen as the administrative point a prisoner from that coast would pass through. It is this file's choice, not a source's.
stops.campa: Somewhere in these years he passes out of Greek jurisdiction and into the King's. How is not recorded. One reconstruction has Cnidus changing sides in the long war between Athens and Sparta, and Ctesias caught in the revolt of Pissuthnes against the crown, then taken by Tissaphernes and sent inland. Sardis is where the satrap of Lydia sits and where a man taken on that coast would be brought. Diodorus says only that he was made a prisoner and kept for his medical knowledge. He names no battle and no captor.
suggested_refs: T. S. Brown, 'Suggestions for a Vita of Ctesias of Cnidus' (1978), the origin of the Pissuthnes hypothesis
sources: Dominique Lenfant, BMCR 2012.04.27, review of Llewellyn-Jones and Robson

stops.name: Babylon, seventeen years by Diodorus's count
stops.date_confidence: an open contradiction, left standing. Diodorus 2.32.4 states seventeen years of honour at court. Counting seventeen back from the last event in the Persica gives an arrival near 415 and supports the long chronology. The shorter chronology, preferred by Schmitt and by several handbook summaries, puts his arrival at the accession of Artaxerxes II near 405/404 and treats the seventeen as an exaggeration or a corruption. This file adopts neither: the stop is dated at the short chronology's arrival and the long chronology's capture already stands at Sardis above. Coordinates inherited byte for byte from the canonical Babylon pin used elsewhere in the corpus.
stops.campa: Diodorus of Sicily, reading him three centuries later, writes that the Cnidian was taken in war, kept for his medicine, and honoured by Artaxerxes for seventeen years. Count seventeen back from the last event in his own book and the arithmetic lands near 415. Count instead from the accession of Artaxerxes the Second and it lands near 405, and the seventeen becomes a copyist's slip or an author's boast. The two chronologies cannot both stand. Did he enter the King's service fourteen years before Cunaxa, or in the year Artaxerxes took the throne? Nothing in the ancient record decides it.
stops.quote: Now Ctesias of Cnidus, on the other hand, lived during the time when Cyrus made his expedition against Artaxerxes his brother, and having been made prisoner and then retained by Artaxerxes because of his medical knowledge, he enjoyed a position of honour with him for seventeen years.
stops.quote_source: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 2.32.4, C. H. Oldfather, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica, Book 2, the passage on Ctesias's captivity

stops.name: Susa, physician to the mother, the wife, the children
stops.date_confidence: the office is attested, the location is inference. Strabo 14.2.15 calls him physician to Artaxerxes, without specifying which Artaxerxes; the II is a modern supplement. Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 1-2, has him attending the king's wife, mother and children. Neither names a residence. Susa is used because the court's winter and spring seat is the likeliest setting for the household material Plutarch draws from him, and the coordinates are inherited byte for byte from the canonical Susa pin. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The post is not the king's body alone. He attends Parysatis the queen mother, Stateira the king's wife, and the royal children, which puts a Greek from a coastal town inside rooms no ambassador and no satrap enters. No ancient writer disputes the position, not even Plutarch, who distrusts nearly everything the man wrote. Plutarch reasons from it instead: whatever farrago of tales he put into his book, he cannot have been ignorant of the name of the king he served.
stops.quote: It is unlikely that Ctesias, even if he has put into his work a perfect farrago of extravagant and incredible tales, should be ignorant of the name of the king...
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 2, Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes, chapters 1-2, on Ctesias's standing at court

stops.name: Ecbatana, the summer road
stops.date_confidence: speculative, and marked as such. No ancient text places Ctesias at Ecbatana, or indeed narrates any movement of his between the royal seats. The stop rests entirely on the seasonal pattern of the Achaemenid court and on the assumption that a royal physician travels with the household. Treat it as the weakest stop in this segment; it is kept because the mobility of the court is the material condition of everything he later writes, and dropped detail here would flatter the record. Coordinates inherited from the canonical Ecbatana pin. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: The court does not stay put. In the hot months it climbs to the Median highland and the old capital under the mountain, and a physician attached to the king's household climbs with it. No text places Ctesias on that road: no letter, no anecdote, no later citation. What stands here is the seasonal habit of the Achaemenid court, which moved between Susa, Babylon, Ecbatana and Persepolis by the calendar, and the ordinary duty of the man who kept the royal bodies.
suggested_refs: The seasonal circuit of the Achaemenid court between Susa, Babylon, Ecbatana and Persepolis
sources: No ancient source; the seasonal pattern is standard Achaemenid administrative geography and is not itself evidence about Ctesias

stops.name: Susa, the royal parchments
stops.date_confidence: the claim is attested, its truth is not. Diodorus 2.32.4 reports Ctesias saying he investigated the facts about each king from royal records kept by Persian law. This is Ctesias's own methodological claim, relayed at three centuries' distance by a writer who never saw such records either. No Achaemenid archive of the kind described has been recovered. Place and date are ordering devices; Diodorus names neither.
stops.campa: He claims a source: that the Persians kept written accounts of their ancient affairs by law, and that he went through them king by king before he wrote anything down. If it is true, he is the only Greek historian with archival access to the Achaemenid past. Nothing survives to test it. No Persian record of the kind he describes has been recovered, and the claim reaches us only through Diodorus, who repeats it three centuries later without having seen the books either.
stops.quote: Now Ctesias says that from the royal records, in which the Persians in accordance with a certain law of theirs kept an account of their ancient affairs, he carefully investigated the facts about each king, and when he had composed his history he published it to the Greeks.
stops.quote_source: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 2.32.4, C. H. Oldfather, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: The disputed question of Achaemenid royal archives and Greek access to them

stops.name: Babylon, Parysatis in her own part of the house
stops.date_confidence: the relationship is attested, the setting is inference. Plutarch's Life of Artaxerxes repeatedly makes Ctesias the source for Parysatis's household and her dealings, and Ctesias's own attendance on her is attested at Artaxerxes 1. Plutarch supplies no location for the ordinary run of court life and this file supplies none either; Babylon is used as a canonical seat of the court and its coordinates are inherited byte for byte. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The queen mother is the fixed power of the reign, and the physician is one of the few men with standing to cross into her part of the household. What he learns there fills the last books of the Persica, and later readers complain that it is not history but the inside of a house. Plutarch takes it wholesale anyway, having nothing else to take: which eunuch carried which message, who was given to whom, what was said over a dinner and what was done afterward.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes, for the Parysatis material drawn wholesale from the Persica

stops.name: Cunaxa, the brothers meet
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event, approximate as a place. The battle is dated 3 September 401 BC and conventionally located about seventy kilometres north of Babylon on the left bank of the Euphrates; the exact ground has never been securely identified by archaeology. Coordinates follow the standard modern placement (Wikipedia, 'Battle of Cunaxa'), which is a convention and not a survey. Ctesias's presence with the king's party is attested by Xenophon, Anabasis 1.8.26-27.
stops.campa: On the third of September the younger Cyrus brings his Greeks and his Asiatics up the left bank of the Euphrates, some seventy kilometres north of Babylon, against his brother the King. The exact ground has never been identified: the name survives, the place does not. Ctesias is with the King's party and not with the Greeks, which puts him on the losing side of every Greek account of the day and on the winning side of the battle. Both armies are commanded by sons of the same woman.
suggested_refs: The unlocated battlefield of Cunaxa on the left bank of the Euphrates

stops.name: Cunaxa, the wound through the breastplate
stops.date_confidence: attested by a hostile contemporary, which is the strongest evidential position anything in this file occupies. Xenophon, Anabasis 1.8.26-27, marched with the Ten Thousand, names Ctesias by trade, reports the wound to Artaxerxes through the breastplate, and passes on Ctesias's claim to have healed it. Xenophon elsewhere gives Ctesias no credit at all, which makes the attribution here worth more than a friendly source would be. Date is the battle's own.
stops.campa: Cyrus drives at his brother through the guard and strikes him in the chest, through the cuirass. The wound is not mortal; Artaxerxes will reign another forty-three years. Xenophon, who marched with the Ten Thousand on the other side and thinks little of the Cnidian, still hands him the moment, naming him by his trade and repeating his claim to have closed the king's wound himself. It is the only episode of Ctesias's life reported by a man who stood on that field.
stops.quote: This, according to the statement of Ctesias the surgeon, who further states that he himself healed the wound.
stops.quote_source: Xenophon, Anabasis 1.8, H. G. Dakyns translation, gutenberg.org/files/1170
suggested_refs: Xenophon, Anabasis 1.8.26-27, the earliest datable notice of Ctesias by a contemporary

stops.name: The hill above Cunaxa, a few companions
stops.date_confidence: attested only as Ctesias's own claim, relayed by a doubter. Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 11, has the king thrown from his horse, rising, and taking a nearby hill with a few companions; that Ctesias was among them is Ctesias's account as Plutarch reports it, not Plutarch's independent statement. Plutarch in the same chapter sets Deinon's version against Ctesias's and declines to harmonise them. The coordinates repeat the Cunaxa pin because no source distinguishes the hill from the field.
stops.campa: Struck, the King goes down from his horse. He gets up, and with a handful of men takes a rise of ground nearby and holds it while the fighting runs on below. Ctesias puts himself among the handful; nobody else places him there, and Xenophon, who was on the field, puts nobody on the hill at all. Plutarch relays the scene and then turns on the teller, saying of his long-drawn account of Cyrus's death that it is like a blunt sword, slow at killing the man but killing him at last.
stops.quote: Such is the story of Ctesias, in which, as with a blunt sword, he is long in killing Cyrus, but kills him at last.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 11, Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 11, weighing Ctesias against Deinon on the death of Cyrus

stops.name: Cunaxa, nine thousand or twenty thousand
stops.date_confidence: attested at Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 13, which gives both figures and attributes the second to Ctesias himself. Plutarch in the same chapter sets Xenophon beside Ctesias and treats the two as in conflict. The date is the day after the battle and is an ordering device: Plutarch gives no day for the count.
stops.campa: The next day the dead on the field are counted. The figure carried to Artaxerxes is nine thousand. The physician, who has walked the field, writes that he thought them no fewer than twenty thousand, and puts that in his book: a man inside the winning camp recording that the official number was less than half. Plutarch reports both figures, sets Xenophon and Deinon beside them, and leaves the three of them disagreeing about how many bodies were on the ground.
stops.quote: Ctesias says that it was reported to Artaxerxes as nine thousand, but that he himself thought the slain no fewer than twenty thousand.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 13, Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 13, the casualty figures and the comparison with Xenophon

stops.name: Babylon, the rewards not itemised
stops.date_confidence: the reward is attested at Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 14, which states that the king gave generous rewards to Ctesias and others and specifies nothing further. The swords of Indian iron are a different order of evidence: they appear inside the Indica as a marvel, not as a documented holding, and are tagged reconstruction accordingly. Neither Plutarch nor Photius supplies a place or a date; Babylon and the September date are ordering devices, with the coordinates inherited from the canonical pin.
stops.campa: The King, alive and victorious, pays those who kept him so. Plutarch records that generous rewards go to Ctesias and to others, and does not say what they were: no sum, no estate, no title, no object. The only possession the record names anywhere turns up inside the Indica, and it is entered there as a marvel rather than as an inventory. There is a sword given him by Artaxerxes, and another given him by Parysatis, both forged of an Indian iron that turns away storms and hail when it is planted upright in the ground.
suggested_refs: The Indica's passage on Indian iron and the swords given by Artaxerxes and Parysatis
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of the Indica, livius.org

stops.name: Babylon, the truce that does not hold
stops.date_confidence: the seizure of the Greek generals under truce is attested by both Xenophon and Plutarch. The location of Tissaphernes's camp is not preserved in any source. An earlier draft pinned it at an invented coordinate in Babylonia; that pin has been dropped and the scene placed at the canonical Babylon pin instead, because the court is at Babylon and there is nowhere else to put it. Ctesias's intervention at Parysatis's urging is his own claim, relayed by Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 18. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Tissaphernes invites the Greek generals to a parley under truce and takes them. Clearchus the Spartan and the others are brought in irons to the court. The camp where it happens is not preserved in any source, and this scene sits at Babylon because that is where the court is and there is nowhere else to put it. Ctesias, by his own account, goes to work at once on the prisoner's behalf, and says the queen mother put him up to it. Nobody corroborates the errand.
suggested_refs: Xenophon, Anabasis 2.5-6, on the seizure of the generals under truce

stops.name: Babylon, the comb and the better rations
stops.date_confidence: attested as Ctesias's own claim at Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 18, and reported there with open suspicion of the teller. Plutarch's assessment of Ctesias's self-insertion belongs to Artaxerxes 13, where the argument is that Xenophon, who names Ctesias elsewhere, would have named him at the post-Cunaxa parley had he been there, and names Phalinus instead. Place and date are ordering devices inside the captivity.
stops.campa: What he does for Clearchus is small and physical: he gets him more food than the guards allow, and he gets him a comb. The Spartan, who has been in irons long enough to want one, is grateful out of all proportion to the size of the favour. Plutarch sets the whole of it down and then, in the same breath, weighs the man who told it to him, arguing that Xenophon would have named Ctesias at the parley after the battle had he been anywhere near it, and names another man instead. No other source mentions the comb.
stops.quote: Ctesias, being prodigiously ambitious, as it would seem, and none the less partial to Sparta and to Clearchus, always allows considerable space in his narrative for himself...
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 13, Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 13 and 18, on Ctesias's self-placement in the Clearchus episode

stops.name: Babylon, the knife in the meat
stops.date_confidence: attested only as Ctesias's own narration, preserved at Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 18, and repeated there without endorsement. Whether the knife was sent, arrived, or was used is not recorded anywhere. Place and date are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Condemned and waiting, Clearchus asks for a way out that belongs to him. Ctesias says he proposed smuggling in a knife hidden inside a piece of salt pork, so the general could take his death from his own hand rather than from the King's executioner. Plutarch repeats it and vouches for nothing. Whether the knife was ever sent, whether it arrived, whether it was used, the record does not say. Clearchus dies by the King's order in the end, and by somebody else's hand.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 18, the bacon-and-knife detail attributed to Ctesias

stops.name: Babylon, the ring of dancing Caryatids
stops.date_confidence: attested at Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 18: Clearchus gives Ctesias his signet, engraved with a group of dancing Caryatids, as a token for his relatives and friends at Sparta. Whether it reached them is nowhere recorded. Place and date are ordering devices; Plutarch supplies neither.
stops.campa: Before the end the Spartan gives the physician his seal, a stone cut with a ring of dancing Caryatids, and asks that it reach his relatives and his friends at Sparta. It is a commission from a condemned man to a foreigner in the pay of the power condemning him, and Ctesias takes it. Four years later he will be at Sparta himself, and Photius lists that visit without saying what he did there. Did the seal ever reach the family it was cut for? Plutarch does not say, and nobody after him says either.
suggested_refs: The signet of Clearchus, engraved with dancing Caryatids, last attested in Ctesias's hands

stops.name: Babylon, the wind and the dates
stops.date_confidence: attested in two independent lines of transmission, both running back through Ctesias. Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 18, gives the wind, the earth, the fallen dates and the grove; Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72 section 72.49, itemises Clearchus's tomb with palm trees among the contents of the Persica. An earlier draft of this file made Parysatis arrange the planting in secret. Plutarch has no such thing: the grove is a spontaneous marvel, and the Parysatis detail has been removed. Place and date are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Clearchus is executed. In the version Ctesias tells, the body lies where it falls until a blast of wind carries a great mass of earth and heaps it over him; dates fall scattered on the mound, and in a short time a grove of palms stands over the grave. No one plants them. Plutarch keeps the story whole, and Photius, epitomising the Persica nine centuries later, still finds the palm trees on Clearchus's tomb worth itemising among the contents of the book.
stops.quote: a blast of wind carried a great mass of earth and heaped it in a mound which covered his body; upon this some dates fell here and there, and in a short time a wonderful grove of trees sprang up.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 18, Bernadotte Perrin, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72 section 72.49, listing Clearchus's tomb and its palms

stops.name: Babylon, the Carian who claimed the blow
stops.date_confidence: attested at Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 14, drawn there from Ctesias. Plutarch names no place and no date for the execution, and Babylon is used as the canonical court pin with coordinates inherited byte for byte. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: A Carian soldier is credited with the wound that finished Cyrus, and Artaxerxes rewards him for it in public. Parysatis wants him for exactly the same reason, and asks. She is given him, and what is done to him afterwards Ctesias sets down without abbreviating anything. The queen mother is taking her son's killers one at a time, in order, with the King's consent where she can get it and around him where she cannot. Plutarch has the whole sequence from the physician who was attending her while she did it.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 14, on the Carian and the king's rewards

stops.name: Susa, Mithridates at the banquet
stops.date_confidence: attested at Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 15, as Ctesias's own narration. Plutarch supplies no location; Susa is inference and its coordinates are inherited from the canonical pin. The date is an ordering device. Note that this passage is the single most-cited exhibit in the ancient and modern case that Ctesias wrote for effect, and that Plutarch reproduces it in full while making that case.
stops.campa: Mithridates, who threw the dart that unhorsed Cyrus, is made drunk at a dinner and boasts of it in front of people who carry the boast back to the queen mother. Parysatis asks for him and is given him. This is the passage of the Persica that later readers hold up when they want to prove the Cnidian wrote for effect, and Plutarch reproduces it whole regardless, marking the account as Ctesias's and not his own: seventeen days, two boats, milk and honey poured into the mouth, and the flies.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 15, the death of Mithridates as told by Ctesias

stops.name: Susa, the knife smeared on one side
stops.date_confidence: attested at Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 19, drawn from Ctesias. Plutarch names no residence, and this file hedges between Susa and Babylon exactly as the sources do; Susa is chosen and the coordinates inherited from the canonical pin. Ctesias's own position, as physician to both women, is attested at Artaxerxes 1 and is what makes his account first-hand in principle and unverifiable in fact. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Stateira eats with her mother-in-law and dies. The bird is carved between them with a little knife smeared with poison on one side, so that the queen mother takes her half unharmed and the King's wife takes hers and does not last the night. Plutarch has the whole account from Ctesias and marks it as his. Ctesias is the physician of both women. Where he was while the meal was carved, and whether anyone called him when she began to fail, he never says, and no source thinks to ask.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 19, the poisoning of Stateira

stops.name: Susa, the informants and the objects
stops.date_confidence: the negative fact is attested and is the important one: no source shows Ctesias travelling to India, and Schmitt's Encyclopaedia Iranica article states this outright. The material of the Indica is gathered at the Achaemenid court from Persian and Indian informants and from objects, animals and visitors arriving there. Every Indian stop in this segment therefore sits at the court pin and not in India, on the standing rule that nobody is staged at a place they never went. The dates order the segment and correspond to nothing in the sources.
stops.campa: India reaches him without his moving. The empire's eastern edge touches the Indus, and what comes west along that road comes through the court: tribute, animals, dyes, drugs, merchants, envoys, men who have been there and will say so for an evening's hearing. Ctesias questions them, handles what can be handled, and writes a book about a country he never enters. In some places he names the method. In others he does not, and a reader cannot tell from the sentence which of the two kinds he is holding.
suggested_refs: The Indian tribute and embassy traffic of the Achaemenid court, the actual catchment of the Indica
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of the Indica, livius.org
Libor Prusa, Graeco-Latina Brunensia, on the biographical evidence

stops.name: Susa, the river taken on report
stops.date_confidence: attested as text, not as observation. The opening geographic claims of the Indica survive through Photius's epitome (livius.org, 'Photius: Excerpt of Ctesias' Indica'). The Indus itself is not a stop on this file: Ctesias never saw it, and the stop is placed at the court where the report was gathered. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He begins with the river. It is immensely broad; the land along it holds nearly as many people as the rest of the world together; rain never falls there and everything depends on the flood. None of this he has seen. A physician's working life is spent certifying what he has examined with his own hands, and here he sets down what other men tell him, in the same voice, without marking the change. He is at Susa the whole time, questioning travellers who have been there.
suggested_refs: Photius's epitome of the Indica, opening chapters on the Indus and the Indian climate
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of the Indica, livius.org

stops.name: Susa, the men who bark
stops.date_confidence: attested as text at Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, sections 37 and 42, in the epitome of the Indica; tradition, not fact, as to the people described. There is no evidence of any biological population answering the description. The stop sits at the court pin because Ctesias never went to the mountains he places them on. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: On mountains near the Indus he places a people the Indians call Calystrii and the Greeks call dog-heads: about a hundred and twenty thousand of them, human in body, canine in skull, dark-skinned, with teeth larger than a dog's and nails curved like claws, and tails above the hips longer and hairier than a dog's. They understand the speech of the Indians and answer in barks and hand signs. A census figure is an odd thing for a fabulist to trouble himself with. They keep flocks, and they dry their fruit in the sun.
stops.quote: On these mountains there live men with the head of a dog, whose clothing is the skin of wild beasts.
stops.quote_source: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of Ctesias's Indica, English translation at Livius.org
suggested_refs: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, sections 37-43, the Cynocephali passage, the classical root of the European dog-headed-people legend
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of the Indica, livius.org

stops.name: Susa, the amber and the bows
stops.date_confidence: attested as text at Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, sections 40-41 and 43. An earlier draft of this file understated the tribute: Photius gives 260 talents of amber and an equal quantity of purple dye and a further thousand talents of amber, and the thousand had been dropped. Restored here. Placed at the court pin, dated only to order the segment.
stops.campa: The dog-heads are inside an economy. Every year they send the Indian king two hundred and sixty talents of amber, as much again in purple dye, and a thousand talents of amber beyond that; every fifth year he sends back three hundred thousand bows, as many spears, a hundred and twenty thousand shields and fifty thousand swords. They live a hundred and seventy years and sometimes two hundred. Photius, copying the figures out in Constantinople, records that they are more just than any other people on earth.
suggested_refs: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, sections 40-43, the tribute, the royal gifts and the lifespan
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of the Indica, livius.org

stops.name: Susa, the martikhora
stops.date_confidence: attested as text in Photius's epitome of the Indica; tradition as to the animal. That Aristotle repeats the creature while marking his doubt is the standard modern account of the Indica's early reception (Karttunen, Nichols) and could not be checked against a primary Aristotelian passage on this pass, so the Aristotle sentence is carried as reconstruction. Pausanias's later guess that the report began as an exaggerated tiger is likewise relayed, not verified. The stop sits at the court pin. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: A red animal the size of a lion, with a man's face, three rows of teeth, and a tail that throws stinging darts: the martikhora, which the Greeks call anthropophagos because it eats more men than it eats anything else. The name is very likely Iranian and means man-eater, one of the places where his ear for the language shows through the Greek. Aristotle will repeat the creature at the Lyceum and record his doubt about it in the same sentence. Pausanias, later still, guesses that the whole report began with a tiger.
stops.quote: The martikhora is an animal found in this country. It has a face like a man's, a skin red as cinnabar, and is as large as a lion.
stops.quote_source: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of Ctesias's Indica, English translation at Livius.org
suggested_refs: Aristotle's zoological notices of the martikhora, repeating Ctesias with reservations
Pausanias's suggestion that the martikhora is an exaggerated tiger
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of the Indica, livius.org
Klaus Karttunen, India in Early Greek Literature

stops.name: Susa, the horn cut into cups
stops.date_confidence: attested as text in Photius's epitome of the Indica; tradition as to the animal and its horn. The identification of the report with rhinoceros accounts, wild-ass lore, or a conflation of both is modern conjecture and is not resolved here. The stop sits at the court pin. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: There is a wild ass in India the size of a horse, white in the body, dark red in the head, blue-eyed, carrying a single horn a cubit long that is white at the base, black through the middle and flame-coloured at the point. Drink from a cup cut out of that horn, he says, and convulsions cannot take you, nor the falling sickness, nor poison. Whether the report began with a rhinoceros, with a wild ass, or with nothing at all, no one has settled. The physician is writing a pharmacology of an animal he has not seen, on the word of men who say they have.
stops.quote: Those who drink out of cups made from it are proof against convulsions, epilepsy, and even poison.
stops.quote_source: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of Ctesias's Indica, English translation at Livius.org
suggested_refs: The horn passage of the Indica, one of the roots of the western unicorn and of the antitoxic-horn tradition
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of the Indica, livius.org

stops.name: Susa, gold in the mountains of the griffins
stops.date_confidence: attested as text in Photius's epitome of the Indica; tradition as to the griffins, and the motif is shared with a wider Central Asian and Greek repertory of monstrous custodians of precious metal. The later transmission through Aelian and Pliny is relayed from the standard modern editions and was not independently verified against a primary passage on this pass. The stop sits at the court pin. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The gold of India is not panned out of rivers as it is out of the Pactolus in his own Asia Minor. It lies in large mountains, and the mountains are inhabited by griffins, which guard it. He does not say whether he takes the guardians for animals, or for what a trading people tell a foreigner who keeps asking where the metal comes from. Was he passing on a warning dressed as a fact, or reporting a beast he believed in? The epitome preserves the claim and not the man's opinion of it.
stops.quote: There is also gold, not found in rivers and washed, as in the river Pactolus, but in many large mountains which are inhabited by griffins.
stops.quote_source: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of Ctesias's Indica, English translation at Livius.org
suggested_refs: The griffin-and-gold motif in Greek and Central Asian tradition, from Aristeas onward
sources: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, epitome of the Indica, livius.org

stops.name: Susa, the letter from Conon
stops.date_confidence: attested at Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, section 72.50, which records the letter from Conon naming Zeno, Polycritus or Ctesias as possible bearers, and records Ctesias adding on his own account a request to be sent to the coast. Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 21, treats the discrepancy between that and Ctesias's own claim that the king assigned him the duty unprompted as evidence of self-promotion. Place is inference: Photius names no residence. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Conon of Athens, beached on Cyprus since Aegospotami, writes to the King asking for a fleet. The letter names three men through whom it may be delivered: Zeno, Polycritus, or Ctesias. Photius, summarising the Persica, records that Ctesias added to the packet a request of his own, that he be the one sent to the coast. Ctesias's own version has the King assigning him the errand unprompted. Plutarch sets the two accounts side by side under his standing charge that the man was prodigiously ambitious.
suggested_refs: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72 section 72.50, on the Conon correspondence

stops.name: Salamis on Cyprus, the letters to Evagoras
stops.date_confidence: attested as correspondence at Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, section 72.50: a letter of Ctesias to Evagoras about reconciliation with Anaxagoras, prince of the Cyprians, Evagoras's agreement to pay tribute, and royal letters and gifts carried both ways. Photius also lists a visit of Ctesias to Cyprus among the closing items. An earlier draft added a separate Cypriot landing pin at Larnaca; no source names a port or a crossing point and that pin has been dropped. Coordinates are the canonical Cyprus pin already in use in the corpus. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He carries the King's correspondence west to Evagoras, who rules at Salamis and shelters Conon. The business is tribute and reconciliation: Photius lists a letter of Ctesias to Evagoras about coming to terms with Anaxagoras, prince of the Cyprians, Evagoras's agreement to pay what the King asks, and royal letters and gifts moving both ways across the sea. A physician is now carrying state correspondence. The fleet these letters assemble will be commanded by an Athenian.
suggested_refs: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72 section 72.50, the Evagoras letters and the tribute agreement

stops.name: Rhodes, the Spartan ambassadors acquitted
stops.date_confidence: attested only in the compressed form Photius gives it, and disputed beyond that. Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72 section 72.51, records proceedings against the Spartan ambassadors at Rhodes and their acquittal. Some modern accounts make this a personal trial of Ctesias for pro-Persian service; the epitome's wording does not support that reading and no source fetched on this pass confirms it. The contradiction is recorded and not resolved. Coordinates are the canonical Rhodes pin already in use in the corpus. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Photius's list gives it in nine words: proceedings against the Spartan ambassadors at Rhodes, and their acquittal. Some modern accounts turn this into Ctesias's own trial, a Greek in Persian pay answering for it in front of Greeks. The epitome does not say that. It says the ambassadors were tried and let go, and it sets the item beside the visits to Cnidus and to Sparta without explaining what any of the three had to do with the others. Nine centuries of copying reduced whatever happened at Rhodes to that one line in a Byzantine reading list.
suggested_refs: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72 section 72.51, and the modern dispute over whether Ctesias himself stood trial

stops.name: Sparta, the visit the epitome names and stops
stops.date_confidence: attested as a bare item at Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72 section 72.50, among the closing contents of the Persica, with no business, purpose or duration recorded. Plutarch's charge that Ctesias was partial to Sparta and to Clearchus (Life of Artaxerxes 13) is the only interpretive frame antiquity supplies. Date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The epitome names Sparta and stops. He has a ring to deliver, or had one four years earlier, and he has spent a decade and a half being the friendliest witness Sparta possessed inside the Persian court. Photius gives the visit one clause, set between the Rhodes proceedings and the return to Cnidus, and attaches no business to it. What he says to the ephors, what he is asked, whether he is thanked or watched, none of it is preserved. Photius wrote down that he went. The Persica breaks off within a year of this visit.
stops.quote: the visit of Ctesias to Cnidus, his native city, and to Sparta
stops.quote_source: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72 section 72.50, English translation at topostext.org/work/237
suggested_refs: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72 section 72.50, the closing itinerary of the Persica

stops.name: Cnidus, the last line of the epitome
stops.date_confidence: attested. Livius.org's overview of the fragments places 'Ctesias returns to Cnidus' last in Photius's sequence, at section 75 of its numbering. That the Persica's narrative ends at Artaxerxes II's eighth regnal year, 398/397 BC, and therefore that the work was composed after the return, is the standard modern reconstruction from the structure of the epitome (Schmitt). Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: The last item in the epitome is four words long: Ctesias returns to Cnidus. He has been gone the better part of twenty years, or seventeen exactly if Diodorus has the figure right. The city that trained him is smaller than the palaces he has been walking through, and its physicians are still arguing with Cos about hips and drugs. The Persica breaks off at the eighth regnal year of Artaxerxes the Second, which is the year he leaves. He writes it here.
suggested_refs: livius.org's fragment overview of the Persica, sections 72.72-75

stops.name: Cnidus, twenty-three books against Herodotus
stops.date_confidence: the book count is attested twice and agrees: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, gives 23 books, and the Suda's own entry on Ctesias (Adler kappa 2521) gives 23 as well. An earlier draft of this file claimed the Suda sometimes gives 24; the Suda entry does not, and the claim has been removed. Note that Strabo 14.2.15 names the works as Assyrica and Persica, not Persica and Indica, and so cannot be cited for the twenty-three-books-plus-one-Indica framing. The Ionic dialect is attested. The place and date of composition are unknown; the pin is his own city and the date orders the segment. That Ctesias positioned himself against Herodotus as a liar is attested in the ancient tradition and is his declared relation to a man a generation older than himself.
stops.campa: Twenty-three books, by Photius's count and by the Suda's alike, written in Ionic, opening on Assyria and running down to the King he served. Herodotus had written the Persian wars a generation before him. Ctesias calls him a liar and a teller of tales and corrects him on the reign of Cyrus and on much besides, from a position no Greek before him had held: inside the palace, on the payroll. The correction has not held; where the two can be tested against Persian evidence, Herodotus is generally the one left standing. The Suda gets the whole career into six words: he wrote Persian Histories in 23 books.
stops.quote_source: Suda On Line, Adler kappa 2521, the entry on Ctesias
suggested_refs: Photius, Bibliotheca cod. 72, on the Persica's twenty-three books and its structure
Lucian, True History, naming Ctesias among the writers of deliberate untruths

stops.name: Cnidus, Ninus and Semiramis before the Persians
stops.date_confidence: attested as content, tradition as to substance. Photius states that books 1-6 treat Assyrian affairs and events before the foundation of the Persian empire, and that the Persian material begins only in book 7; the Assyrian books therefore precede the Persian narrative and are not an appendix to it. Diodorus, Bibliotheca 2.1-20, transmits the Ninus and Semiramis material and cites Ctesias by name at 2.7.1. Nineveh, the legendary Babylon and the siege of Bactra are places the book describes, not places Ctesias went; on the standing rule they are not given pins of their own, and the stop sits at Cnidus, where the book is written. Modern Assyriology does not validate the dynasty or the chronology.
stops.campa: The book does not open where his life did. It opens with Ninus, who founds Nineveh, and with Semiramis, who builds Babylon and adorns it and then marches an army into India and is beaten there, and it reaches Bactra along the way. Diodorus takes the whole of it from him, down to the mound over Ninus, nine stades high and ten wide. Out of these opening books comes the Greek habit of telling the past as three empires in succession, Assyrian, then Median, then Persian. Cuneiform has confirmed none of the king list.
stops.quote: Semiramis buried Ninus in the precinct of the palace and erected over his tomb a very large mound, nine stades high and ten wide, as Ctesias says.
stops.quote_source: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 2.7.1, C. H. Oldfather, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 2.1-20, the Ninus and Semiramis narrative taken from Ctesias
The succession-of-empires scheme in later Greek and Roman universal history
sources: Robert Drews and Reinhold Bichler on the Assyrian books

stops.name: The waters off Cnidus, the fleet comes home
stops.date_confidence: the battle is attested and dated to 394 BC; its location off Cnidus is standard external history and is not drawn from Ctesias. That his own diplomacy with Evagoras and Conon is the antecedent of Conon's Persian command is the reading livius.org's fragment overview supports. Whether Ctesias was alive to hear of it is unrecorded, and livius.org's own remark that he may have witnessed it is a conjecture, not a report. Coordinates are the sea off the cape, not the city pin. The Lion of Knidos named at the end of the campa is attested as an object: a colossal funerary lion found about three miles from the city in 1858 and now in the British Museum. Its connection to the battle is modern speculation and no inscription survives on it; the campa states only the finding and the absence of an inscription, and makes no claim that it is Ctesias's monument. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Three years after he comes home, a Persian fleet under Pharnabazus, with Conon of Athens commanding at sea, meets the Spartans off his own cape and breaks their naval power for a generation. The letters that assembled that fleet passed through his hands at the court and at Salamis. No source records where he was that day, or whether he was still alive to be told about it. The battle takes the name of his city. Three miles from that city a colossal stone lion will be dug out of the ground in 1858, carrying no inscription to say what it marks.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Cnidus, 394 BC, the naval consequence of the Evagoras correspondence
The Lion of Knidos, a colossal funerary monument found three miles from the city in 1858 and speculatively connected to the battle, now in the British Museum

stops.name: Cnidus, and then nothing further
stops.date_confidence: convention, not record. Nothing is attested about Ctesias's death: no year, no place, no manner, no tomb, no epitaph, no cult, no bust, no coin, no gem. The 374-364 range is livius.org's own explicitly labelled educated guess, run backward from an assumed capture near 414 and a normal lifespan; Schmitt's Encyclopaedia Iranica article offers nothing at all. The absence of any ancient portrait is a negative finding from silence across two independent biographical sources, not a source stating the negative. The pin is his own city because there is nowhere else to put him.
stops.campa: After the Persica the record simply stops. No later event is dated to him: no marriage, no pupils, no civic honour, no second journey, no notice of a death. Modern scholarship reckons backward from the probable capture, arrives at a death between 374 and 364, and says plainly that this is arithmetic and nothing else. There is no tomb, no epitaph, no bust, no coin, no gem cut with his face. Five centuries on, Lucian puts him in hell beside Herodotus, among those punished for having written untruly.
stops.quote: the greatest torments of all are inflicted upon them that told any lies in their lifetime, and wrote untruly, as Ctesias the Cnidian, Herodotus, and many other
stops.quote_source: Lucian, True History, Book 2, translation at gutenberg.org/files/45858
suggested_refs: livius.org's conjectural death range of 374-364 BC
The first complete English translation of the fragments, Llewellyn-Jones and Robson, Ctesias' History of Persia (2010), and Stronk's rival edition of the same year
